Mathlib and Std combined have 3 versions of many properties of relations:

Std class Mathlib class Mathlib prop
reflexive relation docs#Std.Refl docs#IsRefl docs#Reflexive
irreflexive relation docs#Std.Irrefl docs#IsIrrefl docs#Irreflexive
symmetric relation docs#Std.Symm docs#IsSymm docs#Symmetric
antisymmetric relation docs#Std.Antisymm docs#IsAntisymm docs#AntiSymmetric
asymmetric relation docs#Std.Asymm docs#IsAsymm
total relation docs#Std.Total docs#IsTotal docs#Total
transitive relation docs#Trans (more generic) docs#IsTrans docs#Transitive
equivalence relation docs#Equivalence (structure) docs#IsEquiv

There are also classes for orders which were upstreamed to core because of the new grind, although the situation here is different because of bundling:

Std class using LE Mathlib class using LE Mathlib unbundled class
preorder docs#Std.IsPreorder docs#Preorder docs#IsPreorder
partial order docs#Std.IsPartialOrder docs#PartialOrder docs#IsPartialOrder
linear order docs#Std.IsLinearOrder docs#LinearOrder docs#IsLinearOrder

I also found docs#emptyRelation and docs#EmptyRelation.

Some relations have instances/theorems for all classes/props, some only for some:

docs#Eq: Equivalence ✓, IsEquiv ✓
docs#Ne: Std.Irrefl x (docs#Ne.irrefl is close), IsIrrefl x, Irreflexive x, Std.Symm x (docs#Ne.symm is close), IsSymm x, Symmetric x
docs#Iff: Equivalence x, IsEquiv ✓
docs#Relation.ReflGen: Std.Refl x, IsRefl ✓, Reflexive ✓
docs#Relation.TransGen: Trans ✓, IsTrans ✓, Transitive ✓
docs#Relation.ReflTransGen: Std.Refl x, IsRefl ✓, Reflexive ✓, Trans ✓, IsTrans ✓, Transitive ✓
docs#Relation.EqvGen: Equivalence ✓, IsEquiv x

I think we should either fill the missing ones and add instances relating everything (already exist for transitive and the order ones) and theorems for the classes to imply the props (already exist for reflexive and transitive), or deprecate Mathlib's classes and props where possible, or at least document this table somewhere.

Thoughts? I assume this has been brought up before but I couldn't find it.

The order classes require more discussion (particularly LinearOrder, which is a mess.)

But personally I would be happy to see docs#IsAntisymm deprecated in favour of Std.Antisymm (and similarly for everything in the first table).

We're close to being done with the (non-order) classes, few last points:

1) docs#Equivalence is a structure and doesn't extend Std.Refl/Std.Symm/IsTrans, so I think we should leave docs#IsEquiv as-is, add an iff theorem between them, and perhaps RFC in core for a new Std.Equiv (though docs#IsPreorder vs docs#Std.IsPreorder might be a blocker)

2) Mathlib's docs#IsTrans vs core's docs#Trans: I suggest changing IsTrans to abbrev IsTrans α r := Trans r r r, but this creates universe problems:

import Mathlib.Tactic.TypeStar
/--
error: Type mismatch
  Trans r r r
has type
  Sort (max 1 u_1)
of sort `Type (max 1 u_1)` but is expected to have type
  Prop
of sort `Type`
-/
#guard_msgs in
abbrev IsTrans (α : Sort*) (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop := Trans r r r

3) lean4#10945 introduced docs#Std.Trichotomous which is ¬r a b → ¬r b a → a = b,
which seems to replace docs#IsTrichotomous but that is r a b ∨ a = b ∨ r b a.
They're of course logically equivalent, but deprecating one for the other seems nontrivial.
Which do you prefer? Should I go ahead and deprecate, or do we prefer mathlib's version and want to suggest it to core?

4) Can I proceed to deprecating the prop versions (e.g. docs#Total / docs#AntiSymmetric)? Their docstrings say e.g. "Std.Total as a definition, suitable for use in proofs", but the classes can also be used in proofs, I don't see a reason to keep them.
cc @Wrenna Robson for trichotomous
We did deliberately choose the version we have there, essentially because it is then the natural counterpart of antisymm.
As I recall Mathlib's version feels like a good idea but in practice it doesn't work amazingly.
I think you probably just want to prove that as a theorem if you don't already have it.
So we should deprecate Mathlib's version, yes?
Yes, I think so.
I am sorry that that is nontrivial. I'm happy to help with review chores and things.
No worries, thanks!

Are we sure we want to be using typeclasses as fields to structures? Now that #35191 is merged, the following code doesn't work:

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Dart

/-- The graph obtained by contracting a dart in an existing graph. -/
def contractDart {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (e : G.Dart) :
    SimpleGraph {x : V // x ≠ e.snd} where
  Adj x y :=
      G.Adj x.val y.val
    ∨ x.val = e.fst ∧ y.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj e.snd y.val
    ∨ y.val = e.fst ∧ x.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj x.val e.snd
  symm := sorry
  loopless
    | x, .inl x_adj_x => G.loopless x.val x_adj_x
    | x, .inr <| .inl x_problem => by tauto
    | x, .inr <| .inr x_problem => by tauto

and one needs to instead do

/-- The graph obtained by contracting a dart in an existing graph. -/
def contractDart {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (e : G.Dart) :
    SimpleGraph {x : V // x ≠ e.snd} where
  Adj x y :=
      G.Adj x.val y.val
    ∨ x.val = e.fst ∧ y.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj e.snd y.val
    ∨ y.val = e.fst ∧ x.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj x.val e.snd
  symm := sorry
  loopless := by
    constructor
    exact fun
    | x, .inl x_adj_x => G.loopless.1 x.val x_adj_x
    | x, .inr <| .inl x_problem => by tauto
    | x, .inr <| .inr x_problem => by tauto
Relevant
FWIW I think the by constructor; exact fun construction isn't so bad if in return we get better interop with core's relation properties and possibly typeclass inference for properties where possible
(I wouldn't be too hopeful for typeclass inference to do too much here, it seems like aesop_graph autoparams is the way to go.)

But yes, I think this extra abstraction barrier is annoying but is less bad than unbundling. Especially since choosing a consistent spelling makes it easier to copy fields between different structures.

Note that where notation also works as:

import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Dart

/-- The graph obtained by contracting a dart in an existing graph. -/
def contractDart {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (e : G.Dart) :
    SimpleGraph {x : V // x ≠ e.snd} where
  Adj x y :=
      G.Adj x.val y.val
    ∨ x.val = e.fst ∧ y.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj e.snd y.val
    ∨ y.val = e.fst ∧ x.val ≠ e.fst ∧ G.Adj x.val e.snd
  symm := sorry
  loopless.irrefl -- <- changed here
    | x, .inl x_adj_x => G.loopless.irrefl x.val x_adj_x
    | x, .inr <| .inl x_problem => by tauto
    | x, .inr <| .inr x_problem => by tauto
Ah yes, I knew I was missing something. Annoying that you must go one deeper, but it's workable with
Transitive #35592

About transivity, we currently have IsTrans (in mathlib) and Trans (from core), and they are separate type classes with a loop like this:

/-- `IsTrans X r` means the binary relation `r` on `X` is transitive. -/
class IsTrans (α : Sort*) (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop where
  trans : ∀ a b c, r a b → r b c → r a c

instance {α : Sort*} {r : α → α → Prop} [IsTrans α r] : Trans r r r :=
  ⟨IsTrans.trans _ _ _⟩

instance (priority := 100) {α : Sort*} {r : α → α → Prop} [Trans r r r] : IsTrans α r :=
  ⟨fun _ _ _ => Trans.trans⟩

Wouldn't it make more sense to avoid the loop and simply make it an abbrev?

abbrev IsTrans (α : Sort*) (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop := Trans r r r

I suppose this would be a breaking change because the argument implicitness in the trans field is different...
I've always thought of Trans as an implementation detail of the trans tactic, I don't think you're really supposed to use it in mathematical code.
Unfortunately I think we do
The trans tactic is in batteries so Trans wasn't made for the trans. Trans is part of the implementation of calc though.

Another case of duplicated relation properties is IsWellFounded and WellFounded, which are the exact same thing, except one is a class and the other isn't. Why don't we replace

/-- A well-founded relation. Not to be confused with `IsWellOrder`. -/
@[mk_iff] class IsWellFounded (α : Type u) (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop where
  /-- The relation is `WellFounded`, as a proposition. -/
  wf : WellFounded r

with

attribute [class] WellFounded

We can still have both APIs for using it as a class or passing it around explicitly.

Is there a particular “plan” for the LinearOrder situation? For example, are we intending to eventually make docs#LinearOrder an alias for <docs#Std.LinearOrderPackage>? Or are they intended to stay as different classes, but with two-way instances, or a one-way instance and constructor, or two-way constructors?

For reference, here are the differences between the packages and Mathlib classes:

  1. LinearOrderPackage uses factories instead of default arguments directly on the type (I’m not actually sure why this is?)
  2. LinearOrderPackage comes with BEq, which is required to coincide with =
  3. The preorder and partial order packages are required to have decidable ≤ and < and = , which is not required in Mathlib
  4. Very different axiomatizations of min/max and compare
  5. Minor field name differences: lt_iff_le_not_ge vs lt_iff, toDecidableLE vs decidableLE

Related to (3) - there are plans to remove this requirement from Mathlib's LinearOrder as well:
#PR reviews > #29422 [LinearOrder α] [DecidableEq α] @ 💬
#mathlib4 > remove decidable fields from LinearOrder?
The above seems to have become #37718 (it adds LinearOrder.ofStd)
Hmm, I wonder what the long term plan should be here. It's of course good to be able to translate between all type classes, but even better would be if we didn't have to do such translations.

A question (because it came up before) - I would personally LOVE to have the definition of Std.Total be ∀ (a b : α), ¬ r a b → r b a. It is just much more nicely symmetric with Asymm and to me is more natural. But I feel like we discussed this before and decided against it - why was that?
We do I guess have Std.Total.rel_of_not_rel_swap and Std.total_of_not_rel_swap_imp_rel
Also, is there a plan to adapt docs#Equivalence to class form? I mean it is bundlled refl + symm + trans essentially.

docs#IsEquiv
As for upstreaming to core, it looks like their queue is super full and they plan to lock down the standard library in July IIRC so I doubt we're going to make it, but creating a PR for lean4#12917 might help
Lock down in what sense?

Of making it very stable and backwards compatible, and they mentioned that adding stuff afterwards would take a lot of convincing first. idk what'll happen exactly, but if now it's very hard to contribute to core I imagine it'll be much much harder in 3 months.
Well, I don't think that's a great idea personally, but oh well.
I think if core was very minimal it would make sense, but it has all sorts of stuff that I would not say is particularly minimal (like this!)

About your comment, I thought things would be moving much faster and so I planned to RFC Std.Equiv only after Std.Trans was accepted, but now I don't think either will make it in time so we might as well try to bunch them together.
What is the source of this claim that the standard library is going to be "locked down" in July?

Possibly it's the Y3 roadmap: https://lean-lang.org/fro/roadmap/y3/ But rest assured that we're well aware that there are still tons of things to do and we're not going to stabilize the standard library in an incomplete state just because we put something into the roadmap a year ago. In fact I believe it's fair to say that achieving stability quickly has been explicitly deprioritized in the past months and that things will continue to be in flux for the foreseeable future.
That is great to hear :)
Well then - would a Std.Equiv be welcome or is the preference to keep things like that unbundled (in that it's really just a combination of Trans, Std.Refl and Std.Symm).

The problem is that Std's relation typeclass are a bit of a mess right now and with these piecemeal changes we are at risk of making the situation even worse. Most of the relation typeclasses have grown over the years without a clear design behind them and I think the time has come to rethink this entire bit of the library from scratch and make all of the changes at once.

As you have guessed, the problem is that no one in the standard library team has the bandwidth to think this stuff through properly right now.

So what would really help would be for the people in this thread who are enthusiastic about the relations API to make one big RFC which approaches the whole topic from the "how to design a good relations API that will last us the next 10 years" perspective with concrete recommendations for how to change the entire thing to be complete and consistent and to integrate well with mathlib and other downstream projects. This RFC should not hesitate to suggest breaking changes. For example this would be the right time to (re)introduce the Is prefix to all of the Prop-valued classes.

Of course I can't promise that we'll follow all of the recommendations, but having an actionable summary of what we can learn from the current implementations in core and mathlib and how we can improve the material in core holistically would be tremendously useful.
Yeah - I mean I was just touching a bit of Mathlib on this yesterday and it quickly became clear that the situation there was sufficiently complex that I gave up
I do hear you about piecemeal changes but sometimes this kind of iterative approach is useful for helping you see what you should have done all along
Whereas a large change all at once I think it is easier to make a wrong decision
(in particular I found a bunch of places where we use docs#Reflexive)
(and I don't even know why we HAVE that really but especially there it really wanted a typeclass)
Note that docs#Transitive is now deprecated in favour of IsTrans
So I don't even know why docs#Reflexive and docs#Symmetric survive
( docs#Reflexive is addressed by #37278 which should be merged soon)

Kevin Buzzard said:

What is the source of this claim that the standard library is going to be "locked down" in July?

The roadmap that was mentioned above says:

Strategy: Our plan is to complete the remaining essential modules—including containers, networking, and asynchronous I/O—and to finalize and document the API. By July 2026, Std will be a stable foundation for future development.

which contains "finalize" and "stable" and "by July 2026". But where I initially got the "locked down" notion from was Leo's talk from Lean Together 2026, where the slides say:

@ Page 54:
Stdlib will be "completed" in 2026 — stable APIs, comprehensive coverage, minimal future breaking changes.
@ Page 55:
2026 will be the last year with significant changes to the language and standard library.
After 2026, we shift to a stability-first approach. Breaking changes will be rare and carefully considered.

This still reads to me as the FRO saying that the standard library will be locked down, and resistant to future changes.
However, while at first what Leo says seems to be pretty much what the slides are saying, with the hindsight of the backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency change (which happened after Lean Together 2026) it now seems that Leo is specifically referring to it. So while the slides are the scary "no more changes to Std", Leo seems to say "no more behavior changes in the language itself". But that wasn't clear at the time.
Also given Julia Markus Himmel's message above, I am now less worried about what those slides warn of. But still both could happen, I guess we'll know in July.
